name: Let's Go Hiking
description:
On a weekend, Qingshan suggests that she and her friend Daniel go hiking. Unfortunately, they are busy high school students, so they can only go hiking on scratch paper. A permutation $$$p$$$ is written from left to right on the paper. First Qingshan chooses an integer index $$$x$$$ ($$$1\le x\le n$$$) and tells it to Daniel. After that, Daniel chooses another integer index $$$y$$$ ($$$1\le y\le n$$$, $$$y 
e x$$$). The game progresses turn by turn and as usual, Qingshan moves first. The rules follow: If it is Qingshan's turn, Qingshan must change $$$x$$$ to such an index $$$x'$$$ that $$$1\le x'\le n$$$, $$$|x'-x|=1$$$, $$$x'
e y$$$, and $$$p_{x'} \lt p_x$$$ at the same time. If it is Daniel's turn, Daniel must change $$$y$$$ to such an index $$$y'$$$ that $$$1\le y'\le n$$$, $$$|y'-y|=1$$$, $$$y'
e x$$$, and $$$p_{y'} \gt p_y$$$ at the same time. The person who can't make her or his move loses, and the other wins. You, as Qingshan's fan, are asked to calculate the number of possible $$$x$$$ to make Qingshan win in the case both players play optimally.
input_specification: The first line contains a single integer $$$n$$$ ($$$2\le n\le 10^5$$$) — the length of the permutation. The second line contains $$$n$$$ distinct integers $$$p_1,p_2,\dots,p_n$$$ ($$$1\le p_i\le n$$$) — the permutation.
output_specification: Print the number of possible values of $$$x$$$ that Qingshan can choose to make her win.
subsubtopic: 472. Grundy Number and Basic Game Theory
approach_summary: Compute Sprague-Grundy values g(u) = mex({g(v) : u -> v}). Game state is winning iff XOR sum of independent game components is non-zero.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1495B — Let's Go Hiking [472. Grundy Number and Basic Game Theory]
topic_editorial.summary: Impartial game theory via Sprague-Grundy theorem.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: Any finite, impartial game under normal play convention is equivalent to a one-pile game of Nim with pile size equal to its Grundy value $g(u) = \text{mex}(\{g(v) : u \to v\})$. A compound game of independent subgames is winning for the first player if and only if $\bigoplus_{i} g_i \ne 0$.
